title: Renewable Deployment
description: LCOE, capacity factors, curtailment, cannibalization, auctions/CfDs, and the grid/permit bottlenecks of deploying wind and solar.

cards.front: What does **LCOE** measure, and what does it hide?
cards.back: Lifetime discounted cost ÷ lifetime discounted output (€/MWh) — the standard cost comparison. It **hides timing and location**: when and where the energy is produced, so it can't fairly compare a variable source with a dispatchable one.

cards.front: Why is **capacity factor** not the same as efficiency?
cards.back: Capacity factor = actual output ÷ output if run at full power all year — it's about **resource and availability**, not fuel conversion. A 20% solar CF means the array averages 20% of nameplate, nothing about panel efficiency.

cards.front: Roughly rank typical capacity factors, highest first.
choices: Nuclear > offshore wind > onshore wind > solar PV
cards.back: Nuclear ~90% > offshore wind ~40–60% > onshore wind ~25–45% > solar PV ~10–25%. Higher, steadier resource (and fewer stops) means a higher capacity factor.

Every added solar/wind unit pushes the price down *in its own production hours* (the merit-order effect), so the technology's **capture price** falls below the market average. Quantified by a declining **value factor**.
**Capture price** = the output-weighted average price an asset actually earns. **Value factor** = capture price ÷ average market price. For solar/wind, VF < 1 and falls as they scale.

cards.front: What is **curtailment**, and why does it rise with penetration?
cards.back: Deliberately cutting available renewable output when the grid can't absorb or move it. As wind/solar grow and hit grid limits, the hours of surplus multiply — a signal that storage, interconnection and flexible demand are needed.

cards.front: A **Contract for Difference (CfD)** mainly does what for a renewable project?
choices: Stabilises revenue around a strike price (and claws back when prices are high)
Guarantees the plant always runs first
Removes the need for a grid connection
cards.back: A CfD pays the gap between a strike price and the market price, and refunds the difference when prices exceed it — revenue certainty for the developer, consumer protection on the upside. That predictability is what lets banks finance it.

cards.front: Why did **auctions** drive renewable costs down so fast?
cards.back: Developers compete to build for the **lowest support level**, so the cheapest, best-sited projects win. Competitive pressure (plus falling tech costs) collapsed bid prices — replacing generous fixed feed-in tariffs.

cards.front: What is today's binding constraint on renewable deployment — and what isn't?
cards.back: **Not cost** (wind/solar are already cheapest). The binding constraints are **grid connection queues** and **permitting/consenting**, plus rising **system-integration costs**. Deployment is grid- and permit-limited.

cards.front: Why **co-locate** (hybridise) solar, wind and storage on one site?
cards.back: It firms the output, raises the **capture price**, smooths variability, and reuses scarce grid-connection capacity — better economics and grid value than a stand-alone variable plant.

cards.front: A 4 MW wind turbine generates 14,016 MWh in a year. Find its capacity factor (decimal).
A solar farm has total annualized cost €1,000,000/yr and produces 20,000 MWh/yr. Estimate its LCOE, €/MWh.
